==Education==
Alavi was born in [[Tehran]] and was educated at the [[University of Cambridge]] where he was awarded a Bachelor of Arts degree{{when|date=January 2017}} in [[Natural Sciences (Cambridge)|Natural Sciences]]<ref name=epsrc>{{cite web|title=Professor Ali Alavi FRS |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20170118154116/https://www.epsrc.ac.uk/about/people/alialavi/ |archive-date=2017-01-18 |url=https://www.epsrc.ac.uk/about/people/alialavi/ |website=epsrc.ac.uk |publisher=[[Engineering and Physical Sciences Research Council]] |location=Swindon |author=Anon |year=2017 |url-status=dead }}</ref> followed by a PhD in 1990<ref>{{cite thesis|degree=PhD|publisher=University of Cambridge|title=Molecular-dynamics studies of thin films and charge-transfer|first= Ali|last=Alavi|year=1990|url=http://ethos.bl.uk/OrderDetails.do?uin=uk.bl.ethos.358367|oclc=557291171}}</ref> for research on the [[molecular dynamics]] of [[thin film]]s and [[charge-transfer complex]]es.

==Research and career==
His research is focused on the [[electron correlation]] and the [[Schrödinger equation]]s, combining [[quantum chemistry]] with [[Monte Carlo method]]s, which enable solutions to problems which are very difficult to solve using standard ''[[Ab initio]]'' [[Ab initio quantum chemistry methods|quantum chemistry methods]] alone.<ref name=epsrc/> His research has been funded by the [[Engineering and Physical Sciences Research Council|Engineering and Physical Sciences Research Council (EPSRC)]].<ref name=epsrc/> Before working in Cambridge and Stuttgart, he held an academic post at [[Queen's University Belfast]].<ref name=epsrc/>

==Awards and honours==
Alavi was elected a [[List of Fellows of the Royal Society elected in 2015|Fellow of the Royal Society (FRS) in 2015]]. His certificate of election reads: {{blockquote|Ali Alavi is distinguished for his highly original contributions to the computation of [[Electronic correlation|electron correlation]] effects in atoms and molecules. His idea of using [[Monte Carlo method|Monte Carlo sampling]] of [[Slater determinant]]s constitutes a breakthrough as it circumvents the [[Numerical sign problem|Fermion sign problem]]. He developed [[algorithm|efficient algorithms]] (FCIQMC) for this, which enables the accurate treatment of larger systems than could be handled by any earlier method. He has applied the technique to outstanding [[Quantum chemistry|quantum chemical problems]]. He has also contributed to the study of reaction mechanisms on surfaces and developed a finite-temperature density-functional method which proved particularly useful for metals and metallic surfaces.<ref name=royal>{{cite web |url=https://royalsociety.org |title = Professor Ali Alavi FRS |publisher=royalsociety.org|archive-date=2015-05-02 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20150502130826/https://royalsociety.org/people/fellowship/2015/ali-alavi/ |location=London|author=Anon|year=2015}}</ref>}}

Alavi was also elected a scientific member of the [[Max Planck Society]] in 2013 and a [[Fellow of the Royal Society of Chemistry|Fellow of the Royal Society of Chemistry (FRSC)]] in 2015.<ref>{{cite web|url=http://www.rsc.org/images/rsc-news-june-2015_tcm18-246763.pdf|title=Prestigious honours for members of our community|publisher=rsc.org|author=Anon|year=2015}}</ref>
